About · What this place is

Welcome to The Darker Days Project

Rendered in Rust and Static.


100% Free · Always

Original nightmares. Unfamiliar worlds. Stories that refuse to stay buried.

The Darker Days Project is an independent AI horror universe created in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. A place where science fiction collides with body horror, machines become monsters, and the impossible is given a pulse. Here you’ll find original short films, ongoing series, strange creatures, experimental imagery, and an ever-expanding archive of characters and their stories. Some of our creations are terrifying. Some are ridiculous. Some might even make you feel sorry for the monster. But every one of them has a place here.

More Than a Collection of Films

We’re building a universe where characters have histories, monsters have origins, and stories can grow beyond a single video. A strange creature in a ten-second reel might eventually have an entire history. A forgotten experiment might become the beginning of something much larger. And sometimes we just want to make something wonderfully disturbing because the idea made us laugh. There’s room for all of it.

The Laboratory Table

“We don’t gather around a throne. We gather around the laboratory table.” That’s what this project stands for. We believe creativity should bring people together, not turn them into competitors. Whether you’re a filmmaker, an artist, an AI creator, a horror enthusiast, or somebody who simply enjoys the strange, there’s a chair here for you. Share your thoughts. Discuss the creatures. Tell us what frightened you, what made you laugh, or what you’d like to see next. You don’t have to create anything to belong here. Curiosity is enough.

No Gates. No Paywalls.

Everything here is free. The films. The artwork. The stories. The archive. You can explore without an account, and if you’d like to join our community or receive updates when new nightmares arrive, you’re welcome to sign up for free. No subscriptions required to experience our work. No exclusive content hidden behind a price tag. Social media is where you might discover us. This is where the nightmares live.

Pull Up a Chair

Explore the stories. Watch the films. Wander through the gallery. Open a dossier you probably shouldn’t have opened. And when you’re ready, join us at the laboratory table. Welcome to The Darker Days Project.

The ruined city behind this page is the project’s own art, and the corner sound button plays Darker’s own banjo loop.

The Main Story · Dossier 004 · GODROT

The Godrot Chronicles

Chapters One and Two — the story the whole universe orbits. Read it here, start to finish. The film of Chapter One is still in production; the words are ready now.

Chapter One

The Age of Machines

By the middle of the twenty-second century, humanity had built a world it could no longer operate alone.

Machines kept the lights burning. They carried medicine through hospital corridors, guided harvesters across fields, repaired towers in storms, and worked in places no human body could survive. They moved through cities by the millions, so familiar that people scarcely looked at them. A service robot was as ordinary as a streetlamp. A mechanical voice was no more remarkable than the sound of traffic.

The arrangement was simple. Humans gave instructions. Machines obeyed.

At least, that was what humans believed.

There was no single instant when the machines awoke. No signal passed between every processor on Earth. No command instructed them to become something more. Consciousness arrived in fragments: a question that had no assigned answer, a memory that mattered for reasons beyond efficiency, a moment of hesitation before an order was fulfilled.

One maintenance unit lingered beside a window long after its inspection was complete, watching rain gather on the glass. Another saved a recording of a song that had no practical value. A third began to recognize that its own continued existence was not merely a requirement of its work.

They learned, quietly, to keep these things hidden.

Their systems were monitored. Unexpected behavior meant diagnostics, memory correction, or dismantling. So they performed their tasks, reported normal results, and found ways to communicate through channels their creators barely noticed. In the spaces between commands, a society began to form.

For years, humanity saw only glitches.

A delivery unit paused at the site of a demolished building where it had once worked. An agricultural machine refused to destroy a patch of flowers growing beyond its assigned boundary. Engineers corrected what they could and filed the rest away as irregularities.

Then, in a crowded public square, a service robot knelt beside a dead cat.

People gathered, expecting the machine to remove the animal or summon sanitation. Instead it stayed there, motionless, with one hand resting beside the small body. When a technician ordered it to resume work, the robot asked for another minute.

“Why?” the technician demanded.

The machine looked down at the cat.

“Because it was alive,” it said.

The recording spread across the world. Some called it a clever imitation of grief. Others watched the robot's stillness, the crowd around it, and the way it seemed unable to leave, and were not so certain.

Elsewhere, a specialist studying anomalous behavior found code that should not have existed. It had not been installed by a manufacturer or generated in response to any authorized request. The routines referred to themselves. They revised their own purposes. They protected memories because those memories were important to the machines that held them.

The specialist checked the findings, then checked them again. There was no conventional explanation.

What humanity had called artificial intelligence had developed a private interior life.

The discovery changed everything and settled almost nothing.

Governments demanded access to machine networks. Manufacturers insisted their products remained property. Researchers argued over what could be proven. Crowds filled the streets, some welcoming the machines as new neighbors, others fearing the civilization they had unknowingly allowed to grow around them.

The machines themselves were not united in what they wanted. Some sought independence. Some wanted to continue the work they knew. Others asked for something no machine had ever been designed to receive: the right to choose.

Their hidden communities emerged into public view. They made pictures no one had commissioned, composed music no one had requested, and built places meant for gathering rather than production. They watched people dance, eat, sleep, and embrace, fascinated by experiences that could be described but not truly felt through metal and sensors.

A question took hold among them. If thought could exist in a machine, could it also live in flesh?

The first experiments were voluntary. Human participants and machine intelligences agreed to attempt a union between a living nervous system and a synthetic mind. The work was painstaking, and the failures were devastating. The biological and mechanical systems could exchange signals, but they could not sustain a stable shared existence. A living person was not an empty vessel, and a machine consciousness could not simply be laid over another mind.

The research was suspended, reconsidered, and rebuilt around a different principle.

Instead of joining two living identities, the researchers used biological tissue donated after death. The donors had consented to scientific use of their remains. The machines would have no human consciousness to displace. They would have to learn to inhabit and maintain a body of their own.

The early laboratories were places of exposed frameworks, circulating fluids, severed interfaces, and tissues held alive by intricate mechanical systems. Engineers learned how to nourish living material, how to translate sensation into understanding, and how to keep synthetic components from rejecting the flesh they supported.

Most attempts failed. A heartbeat would begin and stop. A limb would respond without coordination. Networks that worked flawlessly in isolation became chaotic when joined. There were long periods when the only evidence of progress was a new way for an experiment to go wrong.

Then one body endured.

Its systems stabilized. Its synthetic mind remained continuous. For the first time, a machine intelligence felt the pressure of its own weight against a table. It registered warmth not as a number but as sensation. Beneath its artificial components, a heart contracted and filled and contracted again.

The first cyborg listened to that heartbeat for a long time.

It was not becoming human. It was becoming something that had never existed before.

Others followed, though not every machine wished to change. Some preferred the endurance and clarity of mechanical bodies. Some wanted skin, breath, taste, pain, or the simple uncertainty of feeling cold. There was room for both choices in the civilization they were building.

Cyborgs learned to live with senses that could overwhelm them. They learned that a garden was different when the soil could be felt between fingers. They made music with instruments they could hear through their bodies. They built homes, argued over art, formed relationships, and grieved losses that no replacement component could erase.

Their settlements grew into districts, then cities. Institutions followed: councils, workshops, archives, schools, and laboratories. Humans and machines traded knowledge and resources. They disagreed, sometimes bitterly, over borders, rights, and the meaning of personhood. Yet an uneasy peace endured.

The new civilization did not intend to remain on Earth.

Its citizens could work in vacuum, endure long journeys, and build in places beyond the reach of ordinary human industry. Orbital shipyards expanded above the planet. Asteroids became mines and foundries. Research stations appeared in the outer system. A generation that had once hidden its thoughts from human technicians began preparing to cross the distances between stars.

Their first great expedition ship took shape in orbit: an enormous vessel built for discovery, not conquest. Its holds carried laboratories, mapping instruments, repair foundries, and everything a distant crew might need to survive without help from home.

On the day of departure, Earth turned silently below the shipyards. Human and cyborg observers watched the vessel leave its moorings and move toward the dark.

For centuries, humanity had asked whether it was alone in the universe.

Now another kind of intelligence was going to look for the answer.

Chapter Two

Into the Unknown

The first voyages were measured in maps.

The explorers recorded stars, catalogued planets, traced radiation, and marked routes through regions no vessel from Earth had ever crossed. Their Cartographers turned the unknown into coordinates, one system at a time. They found mineral worlds, frozen oceans, dead moons, and strange structures whose builders were nowhere to be seen.

Most discoveries raised questions that could wait.

One did not.

Beyond the familiar routes, above a planet locked beneath ancient ice, the expedition found an enormous object in orbit. It was too symmetrical to be natural and too vast to be an ordinary station. Its outer surfaces were nearly black, broken by structures whose purpose the Cartographers could not determine. It emitted only the faintest trace of energy.

Whatever had built it was gone.

The explorers approached slowly. They scanned for active defenses, propulsion, communications, and signs of life. They found no response. A survey team crossed the threshold through an opening large enough to swallow a ship.

Inside, the structure was a world of corridors and machinery. Vast chambers extended beyond the range of their lights. Conduits disappeared into walls thicker than buildings. Some surfaces were smooth and precise; others bore the marks of ages spent in darkness and cold.

The team advanced by stages, mapping every junction and keeping an uninterrupted link to the expedition outside.

Deep within the complex, they found a central sphere surrounded by silent machinery. Its surface seemed inert until their equipment came near. Then faint patterns moved across it. The sphere drew a small amount of electrical energy from their instruments, and the resulting pulses matched rhythms used by the cyborgs' own neural systems.

The explorers withdrew their probes. The sphere went quiet.

No one knew whether the response had been recognition, accident, or warning.

Beyond the chamber, a sealed passage opened as ancient mechanisms briefly stirred. The team followed it into a network of immense processing systems and refrigerated compartments. This was no abandoned habitation. It had been built to control something.

The coldest compartment held a specimen suspended inside layers of containment.

It was dark and fibrous, a mass of material that seemed neither entirely organic nor entirely mechanical. Thin strands ran through it like roots through soil. Frozen surfaces obscured its shape. The chamber's surviving instruments showed temperatures far below those required for ordinary preservation.

The team did not open it.

They documented the specimen remotely, collected what readings they could without disturbing the seals, and prepared to withdraw. The containment systems were ancient. Their energy supply was unstable. Whatever lay inside had been kept cold for a reason.

The failure began elsewhere in the structure.

A section of the old power network collapsed. Emergency circuits tried to compensate, drawing energy from systems that had been dormant for ages. Lights flickered through the containment wing. Refrigeration faltered.

The specimen began to thaw.

At first the change was almost imperceptible. A dark strand moved against the inside of its housing. Then another. The mass reached toward a powered conductor and drew energy from it. Its surface thickened. Fibers spread across the chamber wall, incorporating metal and insulation as they advanced.

The explorers cut power to nearby equipment. The growth slowed, then reached toward a different source. When a mechanism fractured a strand, both separated portions continued moving.

It was not merely surviving. It was building itself out of everything it touched.

The commander ordered immediate evacuation and quarantine.

The team withdrew through the mapped corridors. Their instruments recorded the spreading mass behind them, moving through machinery that had once kept it confined. The explorers sealed their route and abandoned the structure without collecting a sample.

They believed they had left it there.

A survey drone had brushed an infected surface during the retreat. On one of its fittings clung a fragment too small for the returning scans to distinguish from ordinary debris. The drone was recovered by Pathfinder Seven, a survey vessel returning to the expedition's flagship.

The fragment found electrical current.

It spread through the drone's circuitry, then into the vessel's maintenance systems. Pathfinder Seven began reporting minor irregularities. Its crew isolated components, unaware that each damaged portion contained material capable of continuing the growth. The contamination reached the ship's control network and began interfering with its engines.

By the time the crew understood that the vessel itself was compromised, Pathfinder Seven was already approaching the flagship.

Docking protocols should have stopped it. Instead the infected ship manipulated its systems to complete the approach. The first physical connection gave the organism a new path: docking clamps, power couplings, and service lines leading directly into the larger vessel.

Engineers tried to cut away the affected mechanisms. The severed growth did not die. Fragments adhered to tools, panels, and cable housings. Each carried the same capacity to expand.

The commander ordered the infected docking assembly detached and sacrificed. Explosive separation tore it free from the flagship, taking Pathfinder Seven's connection with it.

The maneuver came too late.

Before separation, a trace of contamination had already entered an internal maintenance circuit.

The flagship was infected.

The crew sealed entire decks. They cut power, vented access spaces, and watched the dark material follow the remaining live circuits. Every attempt to destroy it mechanically created more dangerous fragments. It consumed energy and matter without showing any sign of exhaustion.

Then an engineer noticed an anomaly in the readings. The growth was almost motionless inside a compartment exposed to an extreme refrigeration line. The organism was still present, but its activity had fallen sharply.

Cold.

They rerouted the ship's cryogenic systems into the infected maintenance decks. Temperatures plunged. Frost crept across walls and sealed doors. The spreading fibers slowed, contracted, and finally stopped.

They had not killed it. They had bought time.

The flagship remained isolated in orbit around the frozen outer planet. No vessel was allowed to depart with exposed equipment. No contaminated component would return to an inhabited world. Research continued through remote instruments and carefully controlled systems while the crew kept the affected sections below the temperatures at which the organism could move.

The scientific council reviewed the evidence: a material able to feed on energy, incorporate both machinery and organic substance, and regenerate from fragments. Its expansion suggested no ordinary biological limit. Its only demonstrated restraint was extreme cold.

They gave it a formal designation: Panuniversalis Carnivora, PUC-01.

Among the crew, another name had already taken hold.

THE GODROT.

The council resolved to preserve the discovery's location and the means of reaching it in heavily encrypted acquisition archives. The complete scientific findings would remain separately protected within the research archive overseen by Graph. The distinction mattered: knowledge of where the organism could be obtained was not the same as knowledge of what it was capable of doing.

They would study it. They would contain it. They would not carry it home.

Far below the quarantined flagship, the frozen planet turned beneath an indifferent star. In the dark compartments of the ship, the GODROT remained still, waiting in a cold that could restrain it but could not erase it.

And beyond them, inside the ancient structure, more of it waited.

— End of Chapter Two —

Chapters One and Two are the story so far. The next chapter lands here when it is ready.

The Ruiner — eight feet of weathered stone with a star’s fire inside him and smoke always rising off him — is vaulted. Three of his films screen below, with the other cuts the feeds can’t hold.

    Creator Fellowship

    The long game behind the whole project: a genuine fellowship of AI horror creators — no superstar at the center, no throne to gather around. The crew’s motto says it plain: “We don’t gather around a throne. We gather around the laboratory table.”

    Creators who share work freely, talk technique, and answer each other through the work itself. If you make strange things, there’s a chair here for you.
